provenance.method: Cross-UK assessment-access route assembled from existing nation-specific healthcare communication adjustment Questions and current assessment-pathway evidence. It describes requests and access planning without guaranteeing a particular adjustment or changing the clinical assessment standard.

question: Can I ask for communication or sensory adjustments during an autism or ADHD assessment in the UK?
why_it_matters: The format of an assessment can itself create barriers through communication demands, unfamiliar environments, waiting, sensory load or the need to process questions quickly.
current_understanding: A person can tell the assessment service about communication, sensory, mobility or access needs and ask what can be adjusted. Useful requests may include information in writing, extra processing time, breaks, a quieter waiting arrangement, support to communicate, advance information about the appointment, or discussion of remote versus in-person elements where the service can offer them. The exact legal framework, service policy and available format differ across the four nations and local services, so ND Oracle does not promise that every requested adjustment will be provided or that changing the format can remove requirements needed for a valid assessment. Existing nation-specific healthcare communication/access Questions give the correct jurisdiction route. If an access need prevented meaningful participation, record what happened and ask the service how the assessment can be made accessible or reviewed.
evidence_needed: Assessment-service-specific reasonable-adjustment and accessibility policies across all four UK nations.
Evidence on which remote/in-person adaptations preserve required diagnostic information for different assessment types.
reopening_conditions: National equality/accessibility guidance or assessment-service adjustment policies materially change.
Clinical assessment standards materially change the acceptable use of remote or adapted assessment methods.
dissent: An adjustment should reduce an access barrier rather than predetermine a diagnostic result; accessibility and diagnostic validity need to be considered together rather than treated as competing absolutes.
